newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish budget gap a warning signal, not crisis.
newsitem.headline: Polish budget gap a warning signal, not crisis.

text.p: The temporary hole in Poland's public finances last week was a warning to the finance ministry, but did not signal serious fiancial trouble, analysts said on Thursday.
They said the state's coffers should get much needed relief in the second half of the year as revenues rise along with larger income tax inflows as tax-payers move to higher tax brackets.

"Even though the second half of the year should bring in higher budget revenues, this is a warning signal," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, head analyst of the government's Centre for Strategic Studies (CSS).
The treasury temporarily ran out of money last week and had to delay paying some public sector workers, putting Finance Minister Marek Belka on the defensive.
"We are not threatened by a budget crisis...(and) by Friday all back payments will be made," Belka said on Wednesday.
The amounts involved remain unclear however and finance ministry officials were unavailable for comment.
The rapid decline of inflation over the first months of 1997 reduced inflows to the budget, which, according to analysts, is already tight.

"For the first time in years there is no inflation premium, which increases budget revenues while expenditures stay fixed as written into budget law," said Bohdan Wyznikiewicz, deputy head of the independent Gdansk Institute for Market Economics.

Inflation fell to about year-on-year 15 percent in May from 18.5 percent at the end of last year and some forecast Poland meeting the budget envisioned 13-percent price growth target for this year, a feet not yet accomplished in Poland's seven year economic transformation from central planning.
CSS's Chroscicki said that this year's budget woes were further strengthened by some 1.5 billion zlotys ($464.7 million) of tax deductions coming from tax-reducing donations.

Last year this tax law loop-hole, which allows tax-payers to deduct up to 15 percent of their income through donating gifts to family members, cost the state about 900 million zlotys, Chroscicki added.

After the first five months of 1997, Poland's budget gap reached 53.8 percent of the 12.22 billion zloty shortfall planned for the whole of year, according to preliminary data from the finance ministry.
Budget revenues in the January-May period amounted to 35.3 percent of this year's plan while spending in the same period reached 37.1 percent.
In the corresponding period of 1996 revenues reached 36.1 percent of last year's plan, spending 37.5 percent and the deficit amounted to 51.9 percent.
